arbitrage.body:
+110 at one book and +105 at another is a 3.73% arbitrage on 1,000 staked:

Exact stakes493.98 / 506.02
Locked if both stand, exact37.35
Round stakes490 / 500
Locked if both stand, rounded35.00
Cost of rounding2.35

A stake to the cent is the loudest fingerprint a risk desk reads. This solves for round stakes directly, because rounding a lock afterwards breaks it.

Finding and sizing it by hand

+110 is 2.10 in decimal and implies 47.62%; +105 is 2.05 and implies 48.78%. Together that is 96.40%, under a whole, so the pair is an arbitrage: one over 0.9640, less one, is the 3.73% margin.

Split the 1,000 in proportion to those probabilities: 47.62% over 96.40% of it is 493.98 on the first leg and the rest, 506.02, on the second. On either result the return is 1,037.35, which is 37.35 over the stake.

Rounded to 490 and 500, 990 goes down. The first leg would return 1,029.00 and the second 1,025.00, so the worse of the two, 35.00, is what is locked.

When an arbitrage is worth taking

Only when both bets can be placed at the prices shown. Prices move in seconds; if the second leg is gone by the time you get to it, you hold one bet, not an arbitrage.

Only when both bets will stand. A book that voids one leg as a palpable error leaves the other exposed, so check the rules on obvious mistakes before betting a price far from the market.

With round stakes. The account longevity page explains why a stake to the cent draws attention.

bonus-bet-conversion.body:
A 1,000 bonus bet does not return its stake, so it is worth about half its face value bet naively. Hedged:

Free legHedge atHedge stakeLocked if both standRate
+100-11052447647.6%
+200-2301,39460660.6%
+400-4503,27372772.7%
+1200-140011,20080080.0%

The hedge column is the constraint every guide omits.

The first row, step by step

A 1,000 bonus bet placed at +100 wins 1,000 of profit if it lands, and the stake does not come back. Against it, 524 goes on the other side at -110.

If the bonus bet wins: 1,000 won, the 524 hedge lost, 476 kept. If the hedge wins instead: it pays 476 of profit and the bonus bet costs nothing, so about 476 on either result. That is 476 of cash from 1,000 of bonus, a rate of 47.6%.

Longer prices convert better and cost more to cover. At +1200 the rate is 80.0%, and the hedge needs 11,200 of your own money on the table until the game ends.

When to convert a bonus bet

When a sign-up offer or a promotion pays you in bonus bets and you would rather have the cash. Hedging turns a large share of the face value into money you keep whichever way the game goes, provided both bets are accepted and stand.

When you can afford the hedge. Pick the longest price whose hedge stake you can cover.

Before the bonus expires. Many expire within a week, and an unused one is worth nothing.

breakeven.body:
What each price needs you to hit:

PriceBreak-even win rate
-20066.67%
-11052.38%
+10050.00%
+15040.00%
+40020.00%

-110 both ways needs 52.38%, which is why a 50% bettor loses steadily and a 53% one does not.

A short price, step by step

At -150 you risk $150 to win $100. The decimal price is 1.6667, and the break-even win rate is one over that, 60.00%. Over 100 bets of $150 that means 60 wins just to finish level.

Miss by a little and it shows. With 58 wins the record reads 58%, which sounds good, and the account is down $500. With 62 wins it is up $500.

The long side runs the other way: +150 is 2.5000 in decimal and needs only 40.00%, so a bettor can lose most of those bets and still come out ahead.

When you need the number

Before a heavy favourite or a short-priced prop, see how often it has to land. Short prices feel safe, and the hit rate they need is easy to underestimate.

Against a record, a win rate on its own says nothing. Put it beside the break-even of the prices actually taken: a tipster who hits most of their picks at short odds can still be losing.

With a fair price, a bet is worth taking when the fair probability from a devigged sharp market is above the break-even of the price on offer. The no-vig calculator gives the first number and this page gives the second.

closing-line-value.body:
A bet taken at +110 against a market that closed at -105:

Your price+110
Closing price-105
CLV against the raw close+7.56%

That figure compares two vigged prices and so overstates the real edge, by about the closing margin. Use it to rank bets against each other, not for claiming an edge size. Devigging the closing market first is what the engine does, and it is why closing line value converges far faster than profit.

The same bet, against the fair close

Your +110 is a decimal price of 2.1000. The close at -105 implies 51.22% for your side, and the raw figure is that probability times your price, less one: +7.56%.

But 51.22% still carries the book's margin. Say the other side closed at -115. The two closing prices imply 104.71% together, and taking the margin out leaves your side a fair 48.84%. Against that, the same bet is worth +2.56%.

So the raw close overstates this edge by 5.00 points, most of it the 4.50% the book held at the close. That is why the raw number is fine for ranking bets against each other and wrong for claiming an edge.

When to check closing line value

After every bet that settles, if you want to know whether you are beating the market. A run of positive CLV says the prices you take are good long before the profit can.

When judging a source of picks. A tipster's CLV is harder to fake than a hot month.

Record the other side's closing price when you can, so the close can be devigged. The no-vig calculator shows how that is done.

deposit-match.body:
A deposit match is a loan of turnover, not a gift, and the interest is the hold on whatever markets the terms let you churn through.

The offer: deposit $1000, receive $1000 in bonus funds, clear 10x rollover before anything can be withdrawn.

Break-even hold is the number that decides it. It sits at 5.0%. Churn below that and the bonus survives to the cashier. Churn above it and the bonus was spent before the terms released it.

So the clause that matters is the one listing eligible markets. Both holds below are measured off real two-way prices, not assumed.

What the rollover allowsChurn holdNetMargin
Moneylines4.55%$90.910.45%
Props only12.41%$-1481.20-7.41%

Same headline, same deposit, same rollover, and a swing of $1572.11 between them. The market restriction is the offer. The bonus figure is packaging.

Competitors print one number to two decimals as though it were measured, then bury the eligible-markets line. Where terms push churn into parlays the cost climbs again; our parlay hold prior of 15.0% is a prior, not a measurement, and it is deliberately excluded from the table above.

The arithmetic behind both rows

In this offer the rollover is counted on the deposit and the bonus together: 10 times $2,000 is $20,000 that has to be bet before a withdrawal.

Every dollar through costs the hold of the market it goes through. On moneylines at 4.55% that is $909.09 of expected cost against a $1,000 bonus, leaving $90.91. On props at 12.41% it is $2,481.20, more than the bonus, a loss of $1,481.20.

Break-even is the bonus over the turnover: $1,000 over $20,000 is 5.0%. Any market holding less than that leaves the bonus worth something.

When to work a deposit match through

Before you deposit, not after. The terms that decide it are the rollover multiple, what it is counted on, and which markets count towards it.

When choosing between two offers. A smaller match with an easy rollover can be worth more than a big one that forces you through props or parlays.

When you can bet both sides across books. A low-hold pair churns the rollover for less than any single book's hold.

dutching.body:
300 spread across 3 outcomes so that every result pays the same:

PriceStakeReturns
+120131.83290.03
+24085.30290.03
+25082.87290.03

Every branch returns 290.03 on 300 staked: -9.97, or -3.32%. That is negative here, and it is supposed to be: the prices imply 103.44% of probability between them, and everything above a hundred is the book's margin. Dutching is the same solver as an arbitrage without the locked floor.

So it earns nothing on its own. It is a way of expressing a view you already hold (that the winner is somewhere inside this set) at a known cost. It is not a way of manufacturing an edge. A dutch across outcomes you have no opinion about is a slow donation at a rate you can compute in advance.

How the stakes are found

Each stake is the pot times that outcome's implied probability, divided by the implied probabilities added together. Done by hand for the three prices above, the share column times the 300 pot gives the stakes in the first table:

PriceDecimalImpliedShare of the pot
+1202.2045.45%43.94%
+2403.4029.41%28.43%
+2503.5028.57%27.62%

The implied column adds to 103.44%. Every outcome returns the pot over that total: 300 over 1.0344 is 290.03.

Dutching some of the outcomes

Covering every outcome of a market only pays the margin. The use is in covering the ones you like and leaving the rest. Take just +240 and +250 with $100: their implied probabilities add to 57.98%, so the stakes are $50.72 and $49.28, and either one winning returns $172.46, +72.46. If +120 wins instead, the $100 is lost.

The bet is worth making only if you think the two together win more often than 57.98%. That figure is the whole decision, and it comes straight from the prices.

Dutching to a target profit

To win $50 whichever of the two lands, solve for the pot: the profit is the pot over 0.5798 less the pot, so the pot is 50 times 0.5798 over 0.4202, which is $69.00. Split it by the same shares.

When dutching fits

In markets with many runners, such as a horse race, a golf tournament or a correct score, where you can narrow the winner to a few without knowing which.

When you want one result from several picks rather than a spread of results.

Against the best price on each outcome. Dutching across books at the best price on each lowers the implied total, and if it ever falls below a whole across every outcome, the dutch is an arbitrage.

effective-bets.body:
Stake spread across correlated bets is not spread. Effective bets is the count a book is really holding: n divided by one plus n minus one times rho, where rho is the average pairwise correlation between positions. Independent bets give n_eff equal to n. Everything else gives less.

The correlation used as a starting point here is a prior, not a measurement: rho of 0.15. The measured figure on this book is 0.45. Same bet counts, two columns.

BetsEffective at prior rho 0.15Effective at measured rho 0.45
21.71.4
42.81.7
83.91.9
124.52.0
205.22.1

Read the measured column down. From 2 bets to 20 bets, the effective count crawls from 1.4 to 2.1. Past a handful of correlated positions, adding another buys no diversification. It only adds stake.

That is what a staking rule has to see. A max single of 5% on a bankroll of 20000 caps a lone bet at 1000. The same rule, applied to a book already loaded with correlated exposure, caps it at 409.96. Competitors print the first figure and call the portfolio diversified. They are counting tickets, and tickets are not independent.

One row, worked

Take 8 bets with an average pairwise correlation of 0.45. The bottom of the fraction is one plus 7 times 0.45, which is 4.15, and 8 over 4.15 is 1.93. Eight tickets carry the risk of about 2 independent bets. At the prior of 0.15 the same 8 come to 3.90.

The correlation does the work. At zero, every bet counts in full. As it climbs towards one, any number of bets behaves like a single bet, because they all win or lose together.

Where correlation comes from

Several bets in one game: a side, the total and a player's points all move with how the game goes.

One team across several markets, or several games that share a cause, such as weather on a day of outdoor totals.

Not from an arbitrage. The two legs of an arbitrage are opposite sides of one result, which is what makes the profit fixed rather than risky.

When to count effective bets

Before adding one more position to a slate that is already loaded on one game or one team.

When sizing with Kelly. Kelly assumes each bet stands alone; on correlated bets the stakes add up to more risk than the fraction meant.

When reading a record. A month of correlated wins is fewer independent results than the ticket count says, so it proves less.

expected-value.body:
Offered +120 on a side whose fair probability is 57.34%:

Expected value per unit+26.14%
Break-even win rate45.45%
Worst method's answer+25.65%

The last row is the one that decides. An edge that exists under one devig method and vanishes under another is a modelling artefact, not an opportunity.

The sum, written out

Expected value is what a bet returns on average per unit staked. At +120 the decimal price is 2.20, so a win pays 1.20 units of profit and a loss costs one unit.

Weight each by its chance. The win side is 0.5734 times 1.20, which is 0.6880. The loss side is 0.4266 times one. The difference, +0.2614, is the +26.14% in the table: about $26.14 on every $100 staked, on average, over many bets like it.

The break-even column is the same sum set to zero. At 45.45% the two sides cancel, so any fair probability above that makes +120 worth taking.

When to work out EV

After devigging a sharp book's market, to judge a softer book's price on the same side. The no-vig calculator gives the fair probability this needs.

To rank several plays. The one with the higher EV per unit is the better use of a dollar, before you think about how much to stake.

Before sizing a bet. EV says whether to bet; the Kelly calculator says how much, given the same fair probability.

hedge.body:
A 100 stake at +250 that has since moved. Laying the other side locks a result now, and what it locks depends entirely on the price you can lay at:

Lay atLay stakeLockedReturn on total staked
-400280.00-30.00-7.89%
-250250.00-0.00-0.00%
-140204.17+45.83+15.07%
+180125.00+125.00+55.56%

The direction surprises people: a longer lay price needs a smaller lay stake, so it keeps more. Laying at +180 locks +125.00, while laying at -400 locks -30.00: a loss taken deliberately rather than a profit secured, because covering the position costs more than the open bet stands to make. Hedging does not create value. It converts a variable outcome into a fixed one, and the price of that conversion is whatever the market charges at the moment you ask.

The reason to do it anyway is rarely the money. A position that is too large for the bankroll behind it is worth closing at a cost, and so is one whose remaining upside no longer justifies the account attention it is drawing.

hold.body:
The standard -110 / -110 market:

Implied total1.0476
Hold4.55%

Hold is 4.55%, not 4.76%. The book's take is measured against the money bet, and reporting the overround excess overstates every book's margin.

Working it through

Take the -110 / -110 market one step at a time. Each -110 is a decimal price of 1.9091, so each side implies 52.38%. Together they come to 104.76%, more than the whole of what can happen, and the excess is the book's margin. Hold turns that into a share of the money bet: one minus one over the total, which is 4.55%.

The same thing in dollars. Someone stakes $110 on each side to win $100. The book takes in $220 and pays back $210 whichever side wins, so it keeps $10: 4.55% of the $220 it took.

Four ways one game can be priced:

PricesImplied totalHold
-110 / -110104.76%4.55%
-105 / -115104.71%4.50%
-105 / -105102.44%2.38%
+100 / -120104.55%4.35%

Shading one side, as in -105 / -115, barely moves the hold. Cutting the juice on both sides is what lowers it.

When the hold matters

Before you bet a side, check what the market charges. The hold is what the price costs you on average, and a pick has to beat it before it earns anything.

Across books on the same game, the one with the lower hold hands back more of each dollar, so it is the first place to look for either side.

To find a pair worth acting on, take the best price on each side from different books and work out the hold of that pair. Below zero is an arbitrage; just above zero is a low-hold pair, which the low-hold calculator works through.

kelly.body:
A 57.34% shot offered at +120, on a 10,000 bankroll:

Full Kelly21.79% of bankroll
At quarter Kelly500.00
Share of bankroll5.00%
Binding constraintmax_single

Quarter Kelly, and sized on the least favourable devig rather than the friendliest. Overestimating an edge costs far more than underestimating it.

The Kelly fraction, worked

Kelly stakes the edge over the odds. At +120 the net odds are 1.20 to one. With a fair probability of 0.5734, the edge is 1.20 times 0.5734 less 0.4266, which is 0.2615. Divided by 1.20, that is 21.79% of the bankroll.

Quarter Kelly takes a quarter of that, 5.45%, or 545 on 10,000. The engine stakes 500.00 instead, because a cap on any single bet of 5.00% of the bankroll binds first. That cap is the binding constraint in the table.

Full Kelly grows a bankroll fastest only when the probability is exactly right. Get it a little high and full Kelly overbets; fractions of it give up some growth for a much smaller swing.

When to size with Kelly

When you have a fair probability you trust, from a devigged sharp market, and a price that beats it. Without the first, Kelly sizes a guess.

When you bet many times from one bankroll and want the stake to shrink after losses and grow after wins.

Check the bet is worth taking first: the expected value calculator uses the same inputs.

low-hold.body:
The same market priced at three books. Covering both sides across 2 of them against covering them at the cheapest single book, on 10,000 of turnover:

Split across books+0.010%, costs 1.00
Cheapest single book+3.981%, costs 398.10
Difference397.10

This is a cost calculator, not an opportunity finder. A positive hold is money gone; low hold is cheaper than the obvious way and it is not free. Whether the turnover buys enough rollover progress or account longevity to be worth the cost is your judgement, and a tool that answers that for you is selling something.

Costing one pair by hand

Say the best price on one side is -105 at one book and the best on the other is +102 at another. In decimal those are 1.9524 and 2.0200, implying 51.22% and 49.50%. Together that is 100.72%, a hold of 0.719%.

Staked so that either result pays the same, the hold is what you lose on average per dollar through. On $1,000 of turnover this pair costs $7.19. The same $1,000 at one book pricing both sides -110 costs $45.45, a hold of 4.545%.

When a low-hold pair is worth it

When a deposit match comes with a playthrough requirement. Turning the bonus over on a low-hold pair is the cheapest way through it, and the deposit-match calculator sets that cost against the bonus.

When you want an account to carry ordinary two-sided action, a low-hold pair keeps the cost of that action small.

When the hold goes below zero, the pair is no longer a cost but an arbitrage, and the arbitrage calculator sizes it.

middle.body:
Identical prices, one point apart:

WindowHitsBreak-evenExpected value
2.5 / 3.515.79%4.76%+10.53%
4.5 / 5.54.21%4.76%-0.53%

Break-even is arithmetic on the two prices and depends on no distribution at all, which makes it the honest anchor. The hit rate comes from counting 285 recorded games, a synthetic, shape stated sample shown as an illustration of the mechanism, not a claim about any league.

One middle, in dollars

Take the first window: $110 on over 2.5 at -110 at one book, and $110 on under 3.5 at -110 at another. If the total lands on exactly 3, both bets win and you are up $200. Any other score wins one bet and loses the other: $100 won, $110 lost, down $10.

Break-even is the hit rate where those even out: 10 over 200 plus 10, which is 4.76%. It needs no model at all. At the 15.79% this sample hits, the expected result is 0.1579 times 200 less 0.8421 times 10, or $23.16 on $220 staked, +10.53%.

When to look for a middle

After the line moves past the number you bet. If you took over 2.5 and another book now hangs under 3.5, the gap between the two is a middle you can take.

Around numbers that land often. In American football a margin of 3 or 7 is the obvious one for spreads, and the totals middle calculator prices a middle on a total.

Whenever the hit rate is your own estimate. Break-even is exact, the hit rate is not, so a middle is only as good as the evidence for how often the window lands.

no-sweat-bet.body:
A no-sweat bet refunds the first bet if it loses. Its value is the refund multiplied by how often the refund actually arrives, and it arrives only in the branch where the qualifying bet loses. So the qualifying bet should be a longshot. That is the opposite of most instincts, and the opposite of the right play on a bet-and-get, where the bonus lands whatever happens.

Figures below assume a qualifying stake of 1000 and a bonus-bet conversion rate of 75%. The conversion rate is a prior, not a measurement.

Qualifying priceRefund valueEV
-110375.00329.55
+150450.00450.00
+300562.50562.50
+600642.86642.86

Short price to long price: 375.00 → 642.86, a ratio of 1.71×. The gap between refund value and EV at the short price is the margin paid to place the qualifying bet at all. Longer is not unboundedly better: the long rows here are priced fair, which is a prior. Real longshot markets carry the heaviest margin, so read the long end as a ceiling.

It is not hedgeable. The refund exists only in the branch where the bet loses, and a hedge pays only in the branch where it wins. Hedging buys away the outcome that produces the bonus, and pays a second margin to do it. Competitors print a single bonus value with the qualifying price held fixed. The price is the entire decision.

no-vig-odds.body:
A book offering -145 / +125 is asserting probabilities that sum to more than one. Removing that margin gives the favourite:

additive57.37%
multiplicative57.11%
power57.50%
shin57.37%

Consensus 57.34%, and the four methods disagree by 0.39 points. Every other no-vig calculator returns one number.

Taking the margin out by hand

The favourite at -145 is 1.6897 in decimal and implies 59.18%. The other side at +125 is 2.2500 and implies 44.44%. Together that is 103.63%; the 3.63% over a whole is the margin.

The multiplicative method scales each side down by the total: 59.18% over 1.0363 is 57.11%. The additive method takes an equal share of the excess off each side instead: 59.18% less half of 3.63% is 57.37%. Power and Shin lean the cut toward the longshot, where books tend to take more.

The consensus of the four, 57.34%, is a fair decimal price of 1.744, or -134. A book offering the favourite at better than that is paying above fair; one offering worse is charging for it.

When to devig

Before judging any price as good or bad. Raw implied probabilities include the margin and make every bet look worse, or a soft price look like an edge it is not.

On a sharp book's market, to get the fair probability that the expected value and Kelly calculators need.

When the four methods disagree by more than the edge you think you have. Then the edge is a matter of method, not of price.

odds-converter.body:
The same price in every form:

AmericanDecimalImplied
-2001.50066.67%
-1101.90952.38%
+1002.00050.00%
+1502.50040.00%
+4005.00020.00%

The implied column is vig-inclusive: it is what the price asserts, not a fair probability. Calling it one without devigging first is the most common way to invent an edge that is not there.

Converting by hand

A plus price is what a $100 stake wins. +150 wins $150, so the decimal price, which counts the stake coming back, is one plus 150 over 100: 2.500. The implied probability is one over that, 40.00%.

A minus price is what you stake to win $100. -200 means $200 to win $100, so the decimal price is one plus 100 over 200: 1.500, and the implied probability is 66.67%.

Going back from decimal: below 2.0 the American price is minus 100 over the decimal less one, so 1.80 becomes -125. At 2.0 or above it is 100 times the decimal less one.

When converting helps

When an exchange or an overseas book quotes decimal and you think in American, or the reverse.

When comparing one line across books. Decimal prices compare in proportion, so the gap between two quotes is plain to see in a way minus and plus signs hide.

Before devigging, convert both sides. Their implied numbers include the margin: -110 on both sides adds to 104.76%, and the no-vig calculator takes the margin out.

parlay.body:
A parlay pays the product of its legs. It compounds the margin on each of them too.

A 4-leg ticket, every leg held at 4.55%, pays 12.28 in profit per unit staked. Strip the margin out of each leg and the fair price pays 15.00. Add the stake back to each and the gap between them is a hold of 17.0% on the ticket: 3.7 times the hold on a single leg.

Holding the per-leg figure of 4.55% fixed as a prior, the hold climbs with the leg count:

LegsHold on the ticket
28.9%
313.0%
417.0%
520.8%
624.4%
831.1%

From 8.9% up to 31.1%. Every added leg is sold as upside. It is also margin, charged before the ticket is graded. Past 7 legs the payout is a lottery price and the hold, still climbing, stops being the number that decides anything.

Same-game legs break the arithmetic above. These legs are in one game and are not independent. A team covering the spread makes the over more likely, not less. Books price same-game parlays with a correlation adjustment for exactly that reason, so the independent figure above is an upper bound on what this is worth, not an estimate of it.

Every other parlay calculator prints the payout to the cent and stops there. The payout is the book's number. The fair price is the number that says what the ticket costs.

poisson.body:
A match modelled at 1.6 and 1.2 expected goals:

Home46.66%
Draw24.71%
Away28.63%
Over 2.553.05%
Push on a 3.0 line22.25%
Most likely score1-1 at 11.68%

The 22.25% push is why books quote halves, and it is the row most totals calculators leave out entirely.

Poisson assumes the two sides score independently. They do not: a team two goals down attacks, a team ahead defends, and real scorelines carry more draws and more blowouts than this model predicts. Treat it as one model's opinion, not a fair price.

Where those percentages come from

Poisson gives the chance of each goal count from one number, the expected goals. The chance of exactly k goals is the expected goals to the power k, times e to the minus expected goals, over k factorial. For the home side at 1.6 and the away side at 1.2:

GoalsHomeAway
020.19%30.12%
132.30%36.14%
225.84%21.69%
313.78%8.67%
45.51%2.60%

A scoreline is one row times another. A 1-1 is 32.30% times 36.14%, which is 11.68%, and a 0-0 is 6.08%. Add every scoreline where the home side is ahead and you have the home win; add the ones on the diagonal and you have the draw.

To turn the home win into a price, take one over it: 46.66% is a fair decimal price of 2.143, or +114. A book offering more than that is above this model's fair price, which matters only as far as you trust the model over the market.

When Poisson is the right tool

In low-scoring games where goals arrive one at a time, such as soccer and hockey. It is the standard first model for totals, both-teams-to-score and correct-score markets.

On a whole-number total, where the push is a real outcome and changes what the over and the under are worth.

It is the wrong tool for American football and basketball, where points come in different sizes and the score is not a count of rare events.

profit-boost.body:
A profit boost multiplies profit, not stake. Profit scales with the price, so the same token is worth a different amount on every bet it could be spent on.

Below, the boost and the stake are fixed (50% on a stake of $100), and only the price moves.

PriceBoost addsEV of the boosted bet
-200$25.00$16.67
-110$45.45$23.81
+200$100.00$33.33
+500$250.00$41.67

The shortest price, -200, adds $25. The longest, +500, adds $250: 10x the profit on the same token, and about 2.5x the expected value ($16.67 against $41.67), with every row taking the posted price as fair. Spend a boost on a favourite and most of it is given away.

Competitors print the headline rate and stop, as though 50% were the value. It is the rate, not the value. The value is the rate applied to a price. The EV column carries a prior: that the posted price is fair. Move that prior and the column moves with it. The ordering does not.

Then the part nobody costs in. A boost spent optimally is a boost spent conspicuously. Optimal use puts the token on a long price, near the top of your staking, inside the window the offer runs. That is a visible exception in an otherwise flat book, and an account whose staking carries a visible exception is an account a risk desk can read.

round-robin.body:
Three legs at −110, taken two at a time, is 3 tickets at 25 each: 75 at risk, not 25. That is the first thing the format hides.

Two legs land91.20 back, +16.20
All three land273.61 back
Legs needed to break even2 of 3
Expected profit at fair 50% legs-6.60
Same money on singles-3.38

Both those last two are computed with every leg at a true 50%, so the difference is not luck. It is the margin, charged once per ticket instead of once per bet. A round robin buys a different shape of outcome, not a better expectation.

Following each ticket

Call the legs A, B and C. Taken 2 at a time they make the tickets AB, AC and BC, 25 on each, 75 in all.

If A and B win and C loses, only AB pays. It returns 91.20, so the round is +16.20 on the 75 staked. If all three win, every ticket pays: 273.61 back, +198.61. If only one leg wins, or none, every ticket loses and the whole 75 is gone.

The ticket count grows fast. At the same stake each:

Round robinTicketsAt risk

When a round robin makes sense

When you like several picks and expect one of them to miss. A straight parlay dies with one loss; a round robin by twos still pays when two of three land.

When you want a parlay's payout shape on part of the money and can live with the margin being charged on every ticket.

Check it against singles first. With every leg a fair coin flip, the round robin above expects -6.60 and the same money on singles -3.38. The parlay calculator prices a single ticket.

totals-middle.body:
A middle is a pair of bets on one game: the over at the lower line, the under at the higher one. Both win when the final total lands inside the window between them. Outside it, one side pays, the other loses, and the miss costs the vig.

The lines priced here are 44.5 and 47.5, a window 3 points wide. Break-even is 4.76%: the rate the window must hit for the pair to be worth holding. That is arithmetic on both prices and nothing else: no distribution, no sample, no view on the sport. It is the honest anchor.

The window probability is 9.19%. That one is a normal approximation, and its spread of 13.0 points is a stated prior, not a measurement. Competitors print a figure like it out to the decimal as though it had been observed.

Counting beats a smooth curve. Real scores cluster on the totals a sport actually produces. A curve cannot reproduce a lump, so it moves mass into gaps where finals never land. Count finals, and hold the sample to a threshold first.

ThresholdMinimum
Games in a totals sample400
Games in a margin sample200
Observations on each distinct total8

Totals carry the higher bar: wider support, more distinct finals, each seen less often. Below any of these minimums the counted estimate is noise wearing a decimal point.

The window in dollars

$110 on the over 44.5 and $110 on the under 47.5, both at -110. A final of 45, 46 or 47 wins both: up $200. Anything else wins one and loses one: down $10. Break-even is 10 over 200 plus 10, the 4.76% above.

The normal approximation centres the total at 46 and asks how much of the curve falls within 1.5 points either side. With a spread of 13.0, that is 0.1154 standard deviations each way, which covers 9.19% of the curve. If that figure were right the pair would be worth 0.0919 times 200 less 0.9081 times 10, about $9.30 on $220. It is a prior, so treat that as a reason to count finals, not a result.

When to price a totals middle

When the total has moved since you bet it and another book now hangs the other side a few points away.

When the window covers finals your sport produces often. Count them in a sample that clears the thresholds above before trusting a hit rate.

For a window one point wide, the middle calculator works the same arithmetic on a counted sample.
